title: LOT’S DAUGHTERS GOT THEIR FATHER DRUNK—YES, THAT STORY IS ACTUALLY IN GENESIS
paragraphs:
LOT’S DAUGHTERS GOT THEIR FATHER DRUNK—YES, THAT STORY IS ACTUALLY IN GENESIS
The Bible does not hide the scandals of broken families. It exposes them—and then, generations later, shows us something almost unbelievable: grace can reach a bloodline without ever calling its sin good.
There are Bible stories people put on nursery walls.
Noah’s ark.
David and Goliath.
Daniel surrounded by lions.
Jesus holding children in His arms.
And then there is Genesis 19.
Nobody is painting this one above the crib.
Because after the fire fell on Sodom, after Lot’s wife looked back, after a family escaped a city under judgment...
two daughters entered a cave with their father.
There was wine.
There was fear.
There was a plan.
And before Genesis 19 ends, both daughters were pregnant by their own father.
Yes.
That is actually in the Bible.
Because the most disturbing thing about this story may not be what happened inside that cave.
It may be how recognizable the road into that cave actually is.
Not because most of us will ever commit the particular sin recorded here.
But because many of us know what it is to survive something devastating and then make terrible decisions while afraid.
We know what it is to confuse desperation with permission.
We know what it is to say, “I had no other choice.”
We know what it is to survive the fire...
and still carry Sodom inside us.
That is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Lot had escaped.
But escape is not always the same thing as healing.

Genesis tells us that Lot left Zoar because he was afraid and lived with his two daughters in a cave. Then the older daughter looked at their situation and concluded that their future was disappearing. Their father was old, and in her perception there was no man available through whom they could continue the family line. Genesis records her proposal: they would give their father wine, lie with him, and preserve offspring through him.
The Hebrew makes the intention painfully direct:
לְכָה נַשְׁקֶה אֶת־אָבִינוּ יַיִן וְנִשְׁכְּבָה עִמּוֹ וּנְחַיֶּה מֵאָבִינוּ זָרַע
Lekhah nashqeh et-avinu yayin, venishkevah immo, unechayyeh me’avinu zara.
In straightforward sense:
“Come, let us make our father drink wine, and let us lie with him, so that we may preserve offspring through our father.”
The Hebrew word זֶרַע (zeraʿ) means “seed” or “offspring.” Their stated purpose was survival of the family line.
Notice what Scripture does not do.
It does not praise them.
It does not tell us that God commanded this.
It does not turn desperation into righteousness.
Genesis reports what happened.
That distinction matters enormously.
One of the most dangerous mistakes we can make when reading the Old Testament is assuming that because the Bible records an action, the Bible approves that action.
It does not.
Scripture is often brutally honest about human beings.
Abraham lies.
Jacob deceives.
Judah sleeps with a woman he believes is a prostitute.
David commits adultery and arranges a man's death.
Peter denies Jesus.
The Bible does not need sanitized heroes because the Bible is ultimately not a story about impressive people rescuing themselves.
It is the story of a holy God dealing with sinful people.
And Lot’s family was broken long before they entered that cave.
Earlier in the same chapter, when the men of Sodom surrounded Lot’s house and demanded his visitors, Lot horrifyingly offered his two daughters instead.
That should disturb us.
It should.
The Bible gives us no permission to defend it.
Something was profoundly disordered in this family.
Then Sodom was destroyed.
Their home disappeared.
Their mother was gone.
Their familiar world collapsed.
Now father and daughters were hiding in a cave.
Fear had become the atmosphere.
And fear can become a terrible counselor.
This does not excuse what the daughters did.
Understanding the circumstances surrounding a sin is not the same thing as declaring the sin righteous.
Later biblical law explicitly prohibits sexual relations between close relatives. Leviticus 18:6 states the principle plainly: sexual relations with close kin are forbidden.
So Genesis 19 is not a secret biblical endorsement of incest.
Far from it.
What we are witnessing is a shattered family making sinful decisions after catastrophe.
And there is another detail we must handle carefully.
Sometimes this story is retold as though we know with certainty that the daughters believed every other human being on earth had died.

The actual Hebrew can be understood as saying there was “no man in the land” or “on earth” available to them. Some later Jewish interpretation understood the daughters as believing the destruction had been worldwide like the Flood, but Genesis itself does not explicitly tell us the full extent of what they believed. The safest conclusion is simpler: from their frightened perspective, they saw no legitimate future for the family line.
So they manufactured one.
And there is the knife.
Because human beings are still doing this.
Maybe not in a cave.
Maybe not with wine.
Maybe not through incest.
But we still do it.
God seems too slow...
so we manufacture an answer.
We are afraid of being alone...
so we enter a relationship we know is pulling us away from Christ.
We are terrified of financial collapse...
so dishonesty suddenly starts sounding practical.
We are afraid our marriage cannot be restored...
so emotional intimacy with someone else starts feeling justified.
We feel unseen...
so we return to pornography.
We feel empty...
so we return to the bottle.
We feel wounded...
so revenge starts masquerading as justice.
We feel abandoned...
so compromise begins calling itself survival.
That is one of sin’s oldest lies:
“You have no other choice.”
Lot’s daughters apparently looked at an impossible future and decided they had to create their own solution.
And when fear convinces you that God cannot make a way, sin will happily offer you one.
The first night, they gave Lot wine.
The older daughter went in.
Genesis says:
וְלֹא־יָדַע בְּשִׁכְבָהּ וּבְקוּמָהּ
Velo-yada beshikhvah uvekumah.
“He did not know when she lay down or when she arose.”
The text repeats essentially the same description after the younger daughter does it the following night. Genesis emphasizes Lot’s lack of awareness during the encounters.
Two nights.
Two daughters.
One father.
Two pregnancies.
And then come the names.
The older daughter gave birth to Moab.
The younger gave birth to Ben-Ammi.

The NET Bible notes that Moab sounds like the Hebrew expression associated with “from our father,” while Ben-Ammi means “son of my people.” These sons became ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites, peoples who would repeatedly intersect—and sometimes clash—with Israel throughout biblical history.
Imagine carrying a name that keeps whispering the circumstances surrounding your beginning.
Imagine a family story you would rather nobody mention.
Imagine having something in your ancestry that you cannot rewrite.
Maybe that is why this story reaches farther than we think.
Some people reading this know exactly what it feels like to inherit a story they never chose.
Maybe your father was an alcoholic.
Maybe your mother disappeared.
Maybe adultery ripped your family apart.
Maybe abuse lived behind the smiling family photograph.
Maybe addiction keeps moving from generation to generation.
Maybe you grew up learning dysfunction so early that you thought dysfunction was normal.
Maybe there are things in your family nobody talks about.
Names.
Affairs.
Children.
Prison.
Addiction.
Violence.
Abandonment.
Secrets buried beneath Sunday clothes.
And somewhere inside you is a question you have been afraid to say aloud:
“Can anything clean come out of where I came from?”
Keep reading.
Because centuries after that cave...
a woman walked into Bethlehem.
Her name was Ruth.
And Ruth was a Moabite.
Let that settle.
Moab.
The people whose ancestral beginning Genesis traces back to that terrible night between Lot and his older daughter.
And from Moab eventually came Ruth.
But Ruth's story would not be defined merely by the scandal behind her people.
She turned toward the God of Israel.
She clung to Naomi.
She met Boaz.
Boaz married Ruth.
They had Obed.
Obed fathered Jesse.
Jesse fathered David.
The shepherd.
The psalmist.
The king.
Scripture explicitly traces that genealogy in Ruth 4.
But God was not finished.
Open the New Testament.
Open Matthew.
Start reading the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
Generation after generation.
Then Matthew writes:
Boaz fathered Obed by...
Ruth.
And Obed fathered Jesse.
And Jesse fathered David.
Do you see it?
Genesis gives us a cave filled with shame.
Ruth gives us a Moabite woman walking in faith.
Matthew places Ruth in the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ.
Not because the incest in Genesis somehow became good.
It never became good.
Grace does not rename evil as righteousness.
Grace does something infinitely more beautiful.
God can redeem people and histories touched by evil without ever approving the evil itself.
That is the Gospel-shaped thunder inside this story.
God does not need a spotless human history to accomplish His holy purposes.
He is holy enough to enter histories stained by human sin and bring redemption without becoming stained Himself.
And eventually, into humanity’s long history of rebellion came Jesus Christ.
Not another sinner trying to fix sinners.
The Savior.
The spotless Lamb.
The Son of God.
Jesus did not come because humanity had finally cleaned up its genealogy.
He came because we could not clean ourselves.
That is why the cross matters.
At Calvary, Jesus was not saying sin does not matter.
The cross screams that sin matters.
It cost blood.
It cost suffering.
It cost the life of the sinless Son of God.
But the cross also declares that your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Repentance is possible.
Forgiveness is possible.
Reconciliation with God is possible.
A new life is possible.
You may have done something you cannot undo.
You may carry consequences that prayer will not magically erase.
You may have wounded people.
You may have wasted years.
You may have hidden something so long that hiding has become part of your personality.
But listen carefully:
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve respectable people.
He came to save sinners.
That means you do not have to sanitize your testimony before bringing it to Him.
You bring the truth.
The ugly truth.
The embarrassing truth.
The truth you wish you could delete.
You confess.
You repent.
You stop defending what God calls sin.
And you throw yourself upon the mercy of Christ.
Grace is not God pretending the cave never happened.
Grace is God refusing to let the cave have the final word.
Maybe that is why Genesis 19 had to remain in the Bible.
We would have edited it out.
God did not.
We prefer polished biographies.
Scripture gives us broken families.
We prefer heroes without stains.
Scripture gives us sinners who desperately need mercy.
We hide scandals.
God exposes sin and then shows what redemption can do.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years believing, “If people knew everything about me, they would never look at me the same way again.”
Maybe.
People may change how they see you.
Consequences may remain.
Trust may take years to rebuild.
Biblical grace is not pretending consequences do not exist.
But your deepest question is not whether everybody will approve of you.
It is whether a holy God can forgive you.
And the Gospel answers through the blood of Jesus:
There is mercy for the repentant sinner.
There is cleansing for the guilty.
There is adoption for the outsider.
There is restoration for the broken.
There is a new identity for the person who comes to Christ.
You are not saved because your family tree is clean.
You are not saved because your past is presentable.
You are not saved because you finally became religious enough.
You are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
So stop hiding behind the cave wall.
Bring it into the light.
Whatever “it” is.
The secret relationship.
The addiction.
The bitterness.
The private messages.
The money.
The pornography.
The resentment.
The double life.
The lie everyone believes about you.
The wound you have turned into permission to wound somebody else.
Do not call bondage “coping.”
Do not call compromise “survival.”
Do not call what God calls darkness your personality.
Come to Jesus.
Not when you have repaired yourself.
Now.
Repentance does not mean merely feeling horrible about yourself.
It means turning.
Away from sin.
Toward Christ.
And perhaps the most astonishing lesson from Lot’s family is this:
Your beginning does not possess sovereign authority over your ending.
Jesus does.
The Moabite story did not end at the cave.
Ruth walked into Bethlehem.
And Ruth's name eventually appeared in Matthew’s genealogy leading to Christ.
That does not make Genesis 19 beautiful.
It makes redemption beautiful.
There is a difference.
Never glorify the scandal.
Glorify the Redeemer.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly. But you can make a simple confession of dependence on Christ.
And read the comments of others with mercy.
There are wounded people behind profile pictures.
There are recovering addicts behind smiling photographs.
There are marriages fighting for restoration.
There are prodigals trying to come home.
There are believers exhausted from battles nobody else can see.
Let this become more than a comment section.
Let it become a reminder that sinners do not need another hiding place.
We need Jesus.
There will probably come a night when your past starts speaking again.
A night when shame tells you God could use somebody else, but never you.
Come back and remember Ruth.
Come back and remember the genealogy.
Come back and remember the cross.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Christ alone saves.
But if you genuinely want your online life to glorify God, one practical way to use what He has placed in your hands is to help put biblical truth in front of people who may never walk into a church.
Supporting Gospel ministry is not a substitute for worship, obedience, generosity to your local church, or care for people in need. It is simply one voluntary way of helping truth travel farther.
Stay close for Scripture.
For conviction.
For encouragement.
For biblical truth when culture gets loud.
For reminders of grace when shame gets louder.
For discipleship that keeps pointing beyond Gospel Warrior and back to Jesus Christ.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who stopped going to church.
Invite the believer who is exhausted.
Invite the person who thinks Christianity is only for people with respectable histories.
Invite the skeptic.
Invite the prodigal.
Invite the person who thinks God could never want them after what they have done.
But whatever you do after reading this, do not miss Jesus because the scandal caught your attention.
Lot’s daughters are not the hero of this story.
Lot is not the hero.
Ruth is not ultimately the hero.
We are not the hero.
Jesus is.
Because Scripture is not telling us that brokenness is beautiful.
It is telling us that our Redeemer is greater than our brokenness.
The cave was real.
The sin was real.
The consequences were real.
But so was Ruth.
So was Bethlehem.
So was the genealogy.
And ultimately...
so was the cross.
Your past may explain some of your scars.
It may explain some of your fears.
It may explain why certain battles are harder for you than they seem to be for somebody else.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, your past is no longer qualified to be your god.
Bring the scandal to Christ.
Bring the shame to Christ.
Bring the family history to Christ.
Bring the secret to Christ.
Bring the consequences to Christ.
Bring the pieces you cannot put back together.
And let the Savior who died and rose again decide what redemption can still become.
Because the most unforgettable thing about Genesis 19 is not merely that two daughters got their father drunk and became pregnant by him.
It is that even after human beings create chapters so dark we can barely stand to read them...
God is still capable of writing grace into the generations that follow.
The cave may be part of the story—but in the hands of the Redeemer, it does not have to be the ending.
